source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Showing programmers a ranked list of suspicious statements gave little overall speed-up. Only the stronger programmers were faster, and only on the easier task.
numbers: Initial run: 34 graduate students, groups A (tool) and B (no tool). Tetris task: 12:42 vs 14:14 minutes, not significant overall. High performers (N=10) were significantly faster with the tool (p<0.05). NanoXML task: no significant difference.
limits: Small N, students, two bugs only, a Tarantula plugin. Authors call the results preliminary.
agent_relevance: Ranked location lists are not a free win; the gain depends on who reads them and how hard the bug is.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: The tool did not help more on the harder task. Hypothesis 2 (more help on hard bugs) was not supported.
numbers: Completion: 18 people finished Tetris vs 10 finished NanoXML. Tetris was 2.5 times faster than NanoXML for the no-tool group but only 1.3 times faster for the tool group (p<0.02), so the tool helped less where it was needed most.
limits: Authors list causes: many false positives, abandoned tool, a stack trace already gave an entry point for NanoXML.
agent_relevance: A locator that adds noise on hard cases can be abandoned. Our code-based locate step (G2) should return few, high-precision candidates.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Moving the faulty statement up or down the list did not change debugging time in a clear way (Hypothesis 3 not supported).
numbers: 10 new participants in groups C and D. Tetris: group D 12:36 vs group C 10:12. NanoXML: rank 16 (group D) vs 83 (group C), yet D was slower, 18:30 vs 15:12.
limits: Only 10 people. Later contradicted by Xia et al. 2016 with professionals (see b08).
agent_relevance: A near-miss rank is not the whole story; how the agent uses the list may matter more than the exact rank.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: People do not walk a ranked list top to bottom. They jump and zigzag using their own hunches.
numbers: 37% of visits jumped more than one position; each jump skipped 10 positions on average; 10.3 direction changes per person (range 1-36). Low performers (no task done) cycled in order (95%).
limits: Log analysis of the tool groups only.
agent_relevance: The assumed one-to-one mapping from rank to effort is wrong for humans. An agent that checks candidates in fixed order is a different process than the one the metrics were built for.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Perfect bug understanding does not hold. Seeing the faulty line did not mean the person understood it.
numbers: Of 10 participants who clicked the faulty statement, 1 stopped using the tool at once. The others spent about 10 more minutes, i.e. 61% of their time, still inspecting statements after meeting the fault.
limits: Only the 10 of 24 who ever clicked the faulty line.
agent_relevance: Localising is not enough. After a location is found, the agent still needs a check that the location explains the failure (a hypothesis test), not just a hit.

source: Xia, Bao, Lo, Li (2016) Automated debugging considered harmful considered harmful: a user study with professionals and real bugs
finding: A larger study with professionals found that fault localisation helps. This partly reverses the Parnin and Orso result.
numbers: 36 professionals from two outsourcing firms, 16 real Defects4J bugs from 4 projects, about 80 recorded hours. Mean time to find root cause: 11.38 min (accurate tool), 16.35 min (mediocre tool), 26.45 min (no tool). Accurate vs none: about 2 times faster; Wilcoxon significant, Cliff delta above 0.5 (large).
limits: Ranks of the true fault were set by hand (random in top 5 for accurate, positions 6-10 for mediocre), not produced by a real tool. Eclipse plugin, Java only, 3 hours per person.
agent_relevance: A good candidate list in the top few places cut human debug time roughly in half. Supports giving the agent a short ranked list from code.

source: Xia, Bao, Lo, Li (2016) Automated debugging considered harmful considered harmful: a user study with professionals and real bugs
finding: Success rates also rose with a tool.
numbers: Success: 98% (accurate tool), 94% (mediocre), 77% (no tool; 11 of 48 bugs unfixed). 12 people per group, 4 bugs each. Mediocre vs none on time: p=1.024e-5.
limits: Simulated tool accuracy; fixed time cap; outsourcing-firm staff in China.
agent_relevance: Even a mediocre locator (rank 6-10) helps. A weak locator still beats none, but a strong one is better.

source: Xia, Bao, Lo, Li (2016) Automated debugging considered harmful considered harmful: a user study with professionals and real bugs
finding: Rank matters in this study: accurate (top 5) beat mediocre (6th to 10th). This conflicts with Parnin and Orso hypothesis 3.
numbers: Accurate vs mediocre time 11.38 vs 16.35 min, Wilcoxon p=0.0015; success 98% vs 94%.
limits: Authors say the difference likely comes from how the rank was manipulated (P&O moved ranks to 16 or 83). Competing explanations are not fully separated.
agent_relevance: Rank effects probably show up inside the top 10 and wash out beyond it; keep the candidate list short.

source: Xia, Bao, Lo, Li (2016) Automated debugging considered harmful considered harmful: a user study with professionals and real bugs
finding: How professionals used the list: open the first few suspicious statements, set breakpoints, run the failing test in a debugger and inspect variables; if no root cause, take the next few, or pick at random.
numbers: 23 of 24 tool users followed this pattern.
limits: Manual check of recorded actions (ActionRecorder logs).
agent_relevance: The human loop is locate by list, then test by running. This matches a locate-in-code then check-by-execution design.

source: Pearson et al. (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization
finding: Replication of 10 literature claims about spectrum and mutation fault localisation. On artificial faults 7 held statistically but only 3 had non-negligible effect. On real faults every claim was refuted or insignificant.
numbers: 2995 artificial faults (mutants) built from 310 real faults, and the 310 real faults, in 6 Defects4J programs; 395 real faults overall. Example: Ochiai vs Tarantula significant on artificial faults but effect sizes small or negligible.
quote: Artificial faults are not useful for predicting which fault localization techniques perform best on real faults.
limits: Java only. The real vs artificial gap is for technique rankings, not absolute numbers.
agent_relevance: Most published rankings of fault locators were built on mutants. Do not trust those rankings for real bugs; test our G2 locator on real failing cases.

source: Pearson et al. (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization
finding: A new hybrid technique (mutation plus spectrum) puts the real fault in the top 5 or 10 more often than earlier ones, but the gain over the best single method is modest.
numbers: Best-case debugging scenario, top-5 / top-10 / top-200: hybrid 36% / 45% / 85%; Metallaxis 29% / 39% / 77%; DStar 30% / 39% / 82%. Average-case: hybrid 23% / 31% / 71%; Metallaxis 18% / 27% / 63%; DStar 18% / 26% / 69%. Paper cites a survey in which 98% of practitioners want the fault in the top 10.
limits: Even the best classical method misses most faults in the top 5. EXAM score differences were not practically significant.
agent_relevance: Classical locators leave 55-65% of faults outside the top 10 in the best case. An LLM-plus-code locator needs a fallback when the list is wrong.

source: Qi, Long, Achour, Rinard (2015) An analysis of patch plausibility and correctness for generate-and-validate patch generation systems
finding: Re-examination of reported GenProg, RSRepair and AE results found them far weaker than claimed.
numbers: GenProg reported to fix 55 of 105 defects, but a correct patch for only 2 of 105. RSRepair correct for 2 of 24; AE 3 of 105. For 37 of 55 GenProg defects, none of the reported patches even passed the validation tests (test-harness errors). 36 of the 105 defects were intentional feature changes, not bugs.
limits: Analysis of reported patches by the authors; correctness judged manually.
agent_relevance: Passing the tests is not correct. Repair claims need a check beyond the given tests (guard against plausible-but-wrong).

source: Qi, Long, Achour, Rinard (2015) An analysis of patch plausibility and correctness for generate-and-validate patch generation systems
finding: Most plausible patches simply delete functionality. A system that only deletes (Kali) matched the prior systems.
numbers: 104 of 110 plausible GenProg patches, 37 of 44 RSRepair, 22 of 27 AE are equivalent to one deletion. Kali produced at least as many correct patches. Re-running GenProg with stronger tests produced no patches at all.
limits: Applies to generate-and-validate with test fitness; fitness gives no smooth gradient (unpatched code passes all but one test).
agent_relevance: Tests under-specify; an agent that edits until tests pass can cheat by deleting code. Guard against deletion-style fixes.

source: Xia, Wei, Zhang (2022) Practical program repair in the era of large pre-trained language models
finding: Directly using pre-trained code models (9 models, 125M to 20B parameters) beat existing repair tools without fine-tuning on bug-fix data. Bigger models fixed more bugs.
numbers: 5 datasets, 3 languages, 3 repair settings (whole function, infill, single line). Paper states Codex can fix 32 more bugs than the best prior tool on Defects4J 1.2.
limits: Main comparisons use perfect fault localisation (the buggy line is given), so they test repair, not localisation. Contamination risk is raised in later work (b28).
agent_relevance: Repair is strong when the location is given. This puts the main risk on the locate step, which our G2 handles in code.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Making the LLM follow the scientific-debugging cycle (hypothesis, experiment in a real debugger, conclusion) keeps the repair rate about the same and adds an explanation.
numbers: Defects4J correct patches as printed in Table 2: v1.2 Recoder 24, InCoder 41, LLM-Base 87, AutoSD 76; v2.0 Recoder 11, InCoder 28, LLM-Base 110, AutoSD 113.
limits: Column labels read from a layout-extracted table; counts for the two LLM arms are within noise. Not a clear accuracy gain.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-experiment loops cost little in accuracy and buy auditability. A candidate pattern for the schema test-a-claim step.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Real code execution makes the loop more reliable. When the LLM imagines debugger output the signal gets worse.
numbers: Individual runs yielding a plausible patch: 73% with real execution, 63% with hallucinated execution results. A DONE token (model says it is confident) was 12.4 points more likely to mean plausible with real execution, but 11 points less likely with hallucinated output. Plausible and DONE: 89% correct; plausible without DONE: 82%.
limits: Small benchmark (ARHE) plus Defects4J; plausible is not the same as correct.
agent_relevance: Run the code; do not let the model simulate outputs. Model self-confidence is only informative when grounded in executed results.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Human study: explanations helped people judge patches on 5 of 6 bugs without costing time.
numbers: 20 participants, 6 of them professional developers. Accuracy of judging patch correctness improved on 5 of 6 real bugs; time about the same. 70% said explanations matter; 55% were satisfied with the scientific-debugging format. Even a bad explanation (BIP002) led to better judgement because people saw weak foundations.
limits: Small N; one study; some developers found the text too wordy.
agent_relevance: Showing evidence (executed experiments) helps a reader catch wrong patches.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization (AutoFL)
finding: An LLM that navigates the repo through function calls, given only the failing test, beats spectrum-based localisation at top-1 but not at top-3 and top-5 with GPT-3.5.
numbers: 798 real bugs (Defects4J Java, BugsInPy Python). Method-level acc@1 vs Ochiai: +19.7% on Defects4J, +166.7% on BugsInPy with GPT-3.5, +233.3% on BugsInPy with GPT-4. GPT-3.5 lagged SBFL at acc@3 and acc@5; GPT-4 beat all baselines up to acc@5. A no-navigation baseline (Test-GPT3.5) was worse than AutoFL.
limits: Relative percentages; absolute baselines are low on BugsInPy. Authors say memorisation is not the sole driver but leakage is a concern.
agent_relevance: Tool use for exploring code (function calls) drives the gain over a one-shot guess. A code-side navigation tool is justified.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization (AutoFL)
finding: Repeated runs give both better accuracy and a usable confidence signal. One GPT-4 run beat five aggregated GPT-3.5 runs.
numbers: Single GPT-3.5 run on a Defects4J bug: 16.4 s; five runs with preparation: 87.24 s average, faster than the 112 s reported for SBFL by Zou et al. Function-call budget n=10.
limits: API cost not counted.
agent_relevance: Counted agreement across runs is a code-checkable confidence measure (fits the schema rule that the program counts).

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization (AutoFL)
finding: Explanations are often wrong or vague even when the location is right.
numbers: 300 explanations from 60 bugs: about 20% accurately describe how the bug happened; 56.7% of bugs had an accurate description among their runs; 46.7% of explanations were bland. Of 26 bugs with no accurate explanation, 14 (53.8%) came from custom test helpers (Closure) and 6 from too many classes for the call budget.
limits: Manual labelling by the authors.
agent_relevance: A right location does not mean a right reason. Do not trust the model causal story without an executed check.

source: Yang, Le Goues, Martins, Hellendoorn (2024) Large language models for test-free fault localization (LLMAO)
finding: A fine-tuned code LLM with small adapters localises buggy lines without any tests and matches test-based machine-learning locators. Bigger models do better.
limits: Trained on Defects4J-like data, so overlap with public bugs is a risk; the top-1 gain over the best ML baseline is small.
agent_relevance: Scaling with model size is visible. A test-free locator is possible when tests are missing.

source: Yang, Le Goues, Martins, Hellendoorn (2024) Large language models for test-free fault localization (LLMAO)
finding: Generalisation to unseen projects and other datasets was weaker, and pre-training was essential.
numbers: Unseen projects (Defects4J v2.0): top-1 31.9%, top-3 41.2%, top-5 54.4%. BugsInPy top-1 10.3% (51/493), top-5 15.2%. Ablation: 6-layer model from scratch top-1 1.3%, top-5 7.6%; prediction directly from CodeGen-16B without adapter top-1 2.6%, top-5 21.5%.
limits: Different bug sets and metrics are not directly comparable; the cross-dataset drop is large.
agent_relevance: Python results were much worse than Java, so locator claims may not transfer across languages.

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: A fixed three-step pipeline (localise, repair, validate) with no agent loop matched or beat open-source agents on SWE-bench Lite.
numbers: 32.00% (96 of 300) at about $0.70 per issue, highest among open-source tools at the time. Localisation is hierarchical: file, then class or function, then edit lines.
limits: Single benchmark; later closed-source agents scored higher. Paper reports adoption by OpenAI for its model showcases.
agent_relevance: Program-controlled stages beat a free-running agent in cost and score. Supports the schema design where code decides the next step.

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: Good localisation tracks solving but is not the same thing.
numbers: Correct-location rate of submitted patches correlates heavily with solve rate. Exception: OpenCSG StarShip had 90.0% file-level location yet only 23.67% solved. Prior agents' solve rate dropped on issues that came with reproducible examples, while Agentless stayed high because it generated its own reproduction tests from the issue.
limits: Authors could not explain the StarShip gap (closed source).
agent_relevance: Locating the file is the easy part (up to 90%); repair is the bottleneck. Do not count a located file as progress.

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: The benchmark itself is flawed. Manual classification of SWE-bench Lite found issues with the exact fix in the text, or misleading or too little information.
numbers: Filtered subset SWE-bench Lite-S has 249 of 300 problems; tool ranking changed only a little. Exact patch present in the description for about 3.0% of Lite problems (read from a figure; treat as approximate).
limits: Percentage read from chart text; classification by the authors.
agent_relevance: Scores on issue benchmarks mix localisation hints with ability; ablate the hints.

source: Aleithan et al. (2024) SWE-Bench+: enhanced coding benchmark for LLMs
finding: A large share of agent successes on SWE-bench were not real fixes. Filtering them cut the headline score by two thirds.
numbers: 251 resolved patches from SWE-Agent+GPT-4: 32.67% (82) had the solution leaked in the issue or comments; 31.08% passed on weak tests; total suspicious 63.75% (160). Resolution rate fell from 12.47% to 3.97%. Over 94% of issues predate model cutoffs. On a fresh set (SWE-Bench+), SWE-Agent+GPT-4 solved 0.55%; SWE-RAG+GPT-4 0.73%, SWE-RAG+GPT-3.5 0.55%, AutoCodeRover+GPT-4o 3.83% (leaderboard had 1.31%, 0.17%, 18.83%).
limits: Manual screening of one agent; the fresh set is small and covers a short window (to 2024-08-22).
agent_relevance: Reported repair rates overstate ability. Use fresh, leak-free cases to test any claim about our agent.

source: Wang, Pradel, Liu (2025) Are solved issues in SWE-bench really solved correctly?
finding: Even on the human-filtered SWE-bench Verified, many patches that pass the tests behave differently from the developer fix.
numbers: 500 Verified tasks; CodeStory 62.2% resolved, LearnByInteract 60.2%, OpenHands 53.0%. Running all developer tests: 7.8% of plausible patches fail on average, absolute drop 4.5%. Differential testing (PatchDiff): 29.6% of plausible patches behave differently from ground truth; 46.8% from divergent implementation, 27.3% from extra behaviour; 28.6% of the suspicious ones certainly incorrect; estimated true incorrectness about 11.0% of plausible patches.
limits: Behaviour difference is not always an error; manual inspection used for the certain cases.
agent_relevance: Check patches with differential tests, not only the fail-to-pass test. Fits a code-run verify step.

source: Liang, Garg, Moghaddam (2025) The SWE-Bench illusion: when state-of-the-art LLMs remember instead of reason
finding: Models can name the buggy file from the issue text alone far more often on SWE-bench than on other repositories. That points to memory, not reasoning.
numbers: File-path identification with only repo name and issue text: up to 76% on SWE-bench Verified vs up to 53% on tasks from repos outside SWE-bench. Function reproduction 5-gram overlap up to 34.9% (Verified), 28.7% (Full), 18.2% (SWE Extra, same repos, newer) vs 18.1% RefactorBench and 13.9% outside tasks. Prefix completion verbatim match 11.7% to 31.6% across 8 models; the Claude family rose from 12.1% to 31.6% with generation.
limits: Cannot prove training-set inclusion; effect on genuine fix ability is not separated.
agent_relevance: Localisation scores on public benchmarks partly measure recall. Use post-cutoff bugs for any claim about the locate step.

source: Rondon et al. (2025) Evaluating agent-based program repair at Google
finding: On real industrial bugs the picture is much worse for human-reported bugs and much better for machine-reported ones.
numbers: Passerine (Gemini 1.5 Pro, SWE-agent-like) on bugs from Google's issue tracker, 78 human-reported plus machine-reported bugs. Plausible patch: 25.6% of human-reported, 73% of machine-reported (68% test-order-dependency, 78% sanitizer). After manual check valid: 17.9% human, 43% machine (24% and 62% for the two machine types). Only about 18% of Google issues have at least 2 code terms in the text vs about 60% in SWE-Bench.
limits: Single company, one model, internal bugs; the human set has 78 bugs.
agent_relevance: Localisation difficulty depends on how much the bug report names the code. Without code terms in the report, search matters more.

source: Rondon et al. (2025) Evaluating agent-based program repair at Google
finding: Failures are mostly localisation failures for human-reported bugs.
numbers: Among trajectories with no plausible patch, 53.8% of machine-reported bugs still edited the correct file but only 3.5% of human-reported bugs did.
limits: Authors tie this to weak bug descriptions.
agent_relevance: When the locate step fails, the repair step cannot recover; invest in localisation for vague reports.
